item.description:
# Reverse-a-function drill — 2026-11-22
Target: Windows x86-64 (arg in `ecx`; return in `eax`).
Reverse this short function to equivalent C. There's no `div` anywhere, yet it divides:
```asm mystery: mov eax, ecx mov edx, 0AAAAAAABh mul edx ; edx:eax = eax * edx (unsigned) shr edx, 1 mov eax, edx ret ```
What does it return for 10 and for 100?
---
## Answer
```c unsigned mystery(unsigned x) { return x / 3; } ```
Results: 3 and 33.
## Explanation
- `div` is slow, so compilers replace division by a constant with a multiply by a "magic number": 0xAAAAAAAB ≈ 2^33 / 3 (rounded up). - One-operand `mul` puts the 64-bit product in edx:eax. Taking only edx is already `>> 32`; `shr edx, 1` adds one more, so the total is `(x * 0xAAAAAAAB) >> 33`, which is x × (2^33/3) / 2^33 = x/3. - The magic is rounded up just enough that the result matches the true floor of x/3 for every 32-bit unsigned x. When you see `mul` by a strange constant followed by a shift of edx, work out 2^(32+shift) / constant to find the divisor.
